Chinese festival that celebrates the coming of spring and a fresh start to one’s life. It usually falls between the winter solstice (dongzhi) and spring’s beginning (lichun). During the 15-day celebration, everyone visits the homes of friends and relatives. Dressed in new clothes, visitors come bearing well wishes and gifts. Children look forward to receiving hongbaos – which literally means ‘red packets’ and these are given to children and adults who are not married. These red packets are filled with new dollar bills and represent good fortune for the coming year. As a sign of respect to one’s elders and friends, two oranges must be brought along when visiting. It’s also customary to present oranges with both hands, and for the recipient to present two oranges when the visitor leaves.

Hari Raya Haji, or the "pilgrimage festival", marks the end of a Muslim's pilgrimage to the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia. It is also known as the Day of Sacrifice, which commemorates Prophet Ibrahim's test of obedience in sacrificing his son Ismail. In Singapore, Hari Raya Haji is a public holiday. Hari Raya Haji (Aidil Adha) falls on 10 Zulhijjah, the 10th day of 12th month of the Muslim calendar. The Muslim calendar, unlike the 365-day Gregorian calendar is 11 days shorter, with the months alternating between 29 and 30 days.

Hari Raya Puasa is the most prominent of all Muslim festivals in Singapore. Hari Raya is Malay for "Grand day of rejoicing". It is also known in Arabic as Edil Fitri. It is a celebratory occasion following a month of fasting. The month of fasting is known as Ramadan. According to the Muslim calendar, Hari Raya Puasa falls on the first day of the Muslim month of Shawal. Shawal is the 10th month in the Muslim calendar. The date of Hari Raya Puasa varies each year.

Thaipusam is a Hindu temple festival which falls between January and February annually. Thaipusam is derived from thai which means "10th", and pusam meaning "when the moon is at its brightest". It occurs when the moon is full in the Tamil month of Thai (between January and February). It is a day of prayers and penance. Devotees prepare themselves spiritually with extensive prayer and fasting before performing acts of penance or thanksgiving like carrying a kavadi from one temple to another. Often, sharp skewers are pierced through their tongues, cheeks and bodies as a practice of self-mortification. Thaipusam was a public holiday in Singapore until 1968.

Theemithi (Thimithi) or "firewalking" is done as part of a religious vow in which the devotee promises to walk on fire in exchange for a wish or blessing granted by the Goddess Draupadi. Theemithi is part of a larger ceremony stretching over a two-and-a-half month period where parts of the Mahabharata is re-enacted, totalling up to 18 distinguishable rites.

Total Defence Day is commemorated annually on 15th February in Singapore. The day marks Singapore's fall to the Japanese in 1942. It seeks to remind people of the sufferings endured by our forefathers during the Japanese Occupation. It is also a day to refamiliarise everyone with the modern defence strategy of "Total Defence".
